# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book teaches Earth observation in the order it has to be learned, not the order it is easiest to publish.

Almost every free Google Earth Engine tutorial opens the Code Editor on page one. You paste a script, a green map appears, and you feel like you have learned something. Two weeks later you are asked why your mangrove map put forest on a hillside twenty metres above the tide line, and there is nothing in that tutorial that helps, because it never explained what the numbers in the image physically are.

So this book starts somewhere else. Part I contains no code at all. It answers why we look at the Earth from orbit in the first place, what a satellite is actually measuring when it records a pixel, and how that measurement behaves differently over a leaf, a mudflat and a sheet of water. Only after that do we open the Code Editor, in Part II. That sequence is not a stylistic choice. It is the sequence that six years of teaching this material has shown produces analysts who can debug their own maps instead of asking why the classifier is wrong.

::: {.callout-note}
## Read this next
[How this book differs](00-different.qmd) explains what is here that the free material does not have, and, just as importantly, what the free material does better.
:::

## Who this is for

**Environmental scientists, foresters and marine practitioners.** You know the ecosystem. You need the computation to stop being the bottleneck. No programming background is assumed; Chapter 6 starts from what a variable is.

**GIS professionals moving from desktop to cloud.** Most of what you know transfers. The parts that do not, chiefly the server side execution model, are handled in Chapter 7 before they can cost you a week.

**Developers and data scientists entering the geospatial domain.** Your coding is not the gap. Part I is where your reading should slow down, because a model trained on physically meaningless features will still report 94 percent accuracy.

**Students and trainers.** Every chapter ends with exercises, and the parts map onto teachable blocks. Appendix E gives suggested course shapes for a five week bootcamp and a three day intensive.

## The route through

| Part | Chapters | You finish able to |
|------|----------|--------------------|
| I. Foundations, purpose and physics | 1 to 4 | Explain what a pixel measures and choose the right sensor for a question |
| II. The platform | 5 to 7 | Write and debug Earth Engine scripts with confidence |
| III. Analysis ready data | 8 to 11 | Build composites from optical, radar and terrain sources |
| IV. Feature engineering | 12 to 15 | Turn reflectance into ecologically meaningful predictors |
| V. Machine learning | 16 to 18 | Train, validate and defend a classification |
| VI. GeoAI and impact | 19 to 23 | Use foundation model embeddings and ship a working application |

: Reading pathways {.striped}

Three shortcuts through the material, depending on why you came.

**The minimum viable analyst.** Chapters 2, 5, 8, 9, 15, 16, 17. From nothing to a validated land cover map with a defensible confusion matrix, in one weekend. This route is written in full.

**The GeoAI sceptic.** Chapters 2, 15, 16, 19. Build a classifier the classical way, then rebuild it from satellite embeddings with a fiftieth of the training data, and judge the difference for yourself.

**The person with a deadline.** Chapter 23 first, then work backwards through whatever it depends on.

## How the code works

Every listing is a real file from `scripts/`, generated into the page at build time. Copy any of them into the Code Editor and press Run. Nothing here is pseudocode and nothing is a fragment that only works in context.

The comments inside those scripts are the teaching, not decoration. Where a line encodes a decision that could reasonably have gone another way, the comment says which alternatives exist and why this one won. Reading a script top to bottom should feel like sitting beside someone narrating their reasoning.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Running the code
Open [code.earthengine.google.com](https://code.earthengine.google.com), paste, press **Run**. A free non commercial account covers every chapter except the export heavy parts of Chapter 23. Appendix A covers registration and the Python alternative.
:::


## What this site does beyond being a book

The chapters are the point, but the site around them keeps track of where you are.

Your reading position, chapter completion, knowledge check scores and private notes are all recorded, and the [progress dashboard](dashboard.qmd) collects them. Nothing is sent anywhere unless you sign in; by default it lives in your browser.

Knowledge checks appear at the end of several chapters. They are one question at a time with an explanation after each answer, right or wrong, because the moment just after answering is when an explanation lands hardest.

The **Ask a question** button sits in the corner of every page. It carries the chapter you are reading with it, so you never have to explain where you are. Questions reach me at [rifkynauvalhsp@gmail.com](mailto:rifkynauvalhsp@gmail.com), and I would rather have a badly worded question than a reader stuck for a week.

## Conventions

::: {.callout-note}
## Concept
Background that explains why something works. Skippable on a first pass, worth returning to.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure
A mistake that is easy to make and hard to diagnose. Worth reading even if you skip everything else on the page.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity
A point where technically valid code still produces a scientifically indefensible map.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Something that only shows up in operational work, usually the hard way.
:::

## Acknowledgements

The foundational scripts in Part II descend from the EE101 teaching series by Noel Gorelick, David Gibson, Nicholas Clinton and Hadi, adapted here with gratitude. The mangrove and blue carbon material draws on field data and methodological work from the Indonesian conservation research community, including CIFOR plot data from West Papua. The business location chapter builds on module work by Rafli Ortega Jaya. Errors that remain are mine.
